# Campaign results {#sec-campaigns}

**Of five configurations scored under a ten-fold sampling-density skew on
DrivAerML, only the similarity-gauge ISLA keeps its accuracy (1.21x); in
the frame a biased mesher would deliver, the input-matched unit-drive
GeoTransolver, Transolver and the constant-gauge ISLA all collapse about
twelve-fold and the measure-weights-off ablation nineteen-fold. When every
car arrives in a random pose, ISLA keeps its canonical accuracy (1.4%
worse) while the augmented GeoTransolver and Transolver lose 20% and 31%,
and ISLA leads both. On the one real transfer setting, a few hundred cars
of a sibling family buy the target family almost entirely, a convention
flag buys nothing, and fine-tuning from DrivAerML on 20 fastback labels is
worth 31% for GeoTransolver and nothing for ISLA. In the interior, width
closes ISLA's pressure gap to GeoTransolver-volume at matched parameters
and leaves an eddy-viscosity deficit that lives entirely in the far field
and is not repaired by far-field context tokens.** This chapter collects
the verdicts of the node-budget campaigns (@sec-nb-campaign) as they
close; each section states the question, the preregistered bar, the
float32 readout and what it changes. Every campaign has closed.

## Data-draw variance of the HiLift comparisons (campaign A, 35 and 210 cases) {#sec-campaigns-draws}

Every HiLiftAeroML comparison in the program book rests on one curated
training draw per rung with two or three seeds. Campaign A retrains the
four arms of the 35- and 210-case rungs (unit-drive GeoTransolver,
unit-drive Transolver, ISLA, ISLA without measure weights) on three
independent geometry-stratified draws of training cases, three seeds
each, and asks whether the orderings survive the draw and how much of a
number's uncertainty the seed protocol was missing (@sec-nb-campa-n35,
@sec-nb-campa-n210; preregistration in `studies/campaign_a_draws/`).

```{python}
#| output: asis
import json
from pathlib import Path
d = json.loads(Path("studies/campaign_a_draws/campaign_a_n35_fp32_2026-09-10.json").read_text())
names = {"gt_n35": "GeoTransolver, unit drive", "transolver_n35": "Transolver, unit drive", "isla_n35": "ISLA", "islanw_n35": "ISLA, measure weights off"}
print("| arm | draw 1 | draw 2 | draw 3 | curated draw | between-draw SD ÷ within-draw SD |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for k, n in names.items():
    a = d["arms"][k]; pd_ = a["per_draw"]; dec = a["pressure_decomposition"]
    cells = [f"{pd_[str(i)]['seed_mean']['pressure_l2']:.4f}" if str(i) in pd_ else "—" for i in (1, 2, 3, 0)]
    print(f"| {n} | " + " | ".join(cells) + f" | {dec['ratio_between_over_within']:.1f} |")
print()
print(": Validation surface-pressure relative L2 at 35 training cases, float32 inference, seed means (three seeds) per draw; the curated draw is the program book's split, re-evaluated in float32. Data: studies/campaign_a_draws/campaign_a_n35_fp32_2026-09-10.json. {#tbl-campaigns-draws}")
print()
rn = {"gt_over_isla_n35": "GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA", "transolver_over_isla_n35": "Transolver ÷ ISLA", "noweights_over_isla_n35": "ISLA weights off ÷ ISLA"}
print("| ratio | draw 1 | draw 2 | draw 3 | curated | mean | 90% interval | verdict |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for k, n in rn.items():
    r = d["ratios"][k]; pdr = r["per_draw"]
    cells = [f"{pdr[str(i)]['ratio']:.3f}" if str(i) in pdr else "—" for i in (1, 2, 3, 0)]
    print(f"| {n} | " + " | ".join(cells) + f" | {r['mean_over_draws']:.3f} | [{r['ci90'][0]:.3f}, {r['ci90'][1]:.3f}] | {r['verdict']} |")
print()
print(": Ratios of seed-mean errors per draw; the interval is the two-sided 90% t-interval over the three campaign draws. {#tbl-campaigns-draw-ratios}")
```

Both "ISLA behind" orderings stand: the intervals lie below 1.0 and the
curated draw's ratios sit inside them, so the book's 35-case statements
gain a data-draw interval and lose nothing. The measure-weights-off
ablation's in-distribution gain is draw-dependent, real on average (0.91)
but 0.95 on the hardest draw, so the measure semantics cost 5–10% on
canonical HiLift data depending on the draw; the ablation reads sampling
density and is not a candidate configuration (@sec-nb-redirect). The
number that changes
practice is the variance decomposition: the between-draw standard deviation
of an arm's error is 3 to 11 times its seed standard deviation, and the
hardest draw is 24% harder than the easiest for GeoTransolver, so the
two-seed protocol has been understating the uncertainty of every 35-case
HiLift number by that factor; future rungs need draws, not seeds.

```{python}
#| output: asis
import json
from pathlib import Path
d = json.loads(Path("studies/campaign_a_draws/campaign_a_n210_fp32_2026-09-10.json").read_text())
names = {"gt_n210": "GeoTransolver, unit drive", "transolver_n210": "Transolver, unit drive", "isla_n210": "ISLA", "islanw_n210": "ISLA, measure weights off (ablation)"}
print("| arm | draw 1 | draw 2 | draw 3 | curated draw | between-draw SD ÷ within-draw SD |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for k, n in names.items():
    a = d["arms"][k]; pd_ = a["per_draw"]; dec = a["pressure_decomposition"]
    cells = [f"{pd_[str(i)]['seed_mean']['pressure_l2']:.4f}" if str(i) in pd_ else "—" for i in (1, 2, 3, 0)]
    print(f"| {n} | " + " | ".join(cells) + f" | {dec['ratio_between_over_within']:.1f} |")
print()
print(": Validation surface-pressure relative L2 at 210 training cases, float32 inference, seed means (three seeds) per draw; the curated draw is the program book's split, re-evaluated in float32 (marginally outside the three-draw range for GeoTransolver, by 0.0003). Data: studies/campaign_a_draws/campaign_a_n210_fp32_2026-09-10.json. {#tbl-campaigns-draws-210}")
print()
rn = {"gt_over_isla_n210": "GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA", "transolver_over_isla_n210": "Transolver ÷ ISLA", "noweights_over_isla_n210": "ISLA weights off ÷ ISLA"}
print("| ratio | draw 1 | draw 2 | draw 3 | curated | mean | 90% interval | verdict |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for k, n in rn.items():
    r = d["ratios"][k]; pdr = r["per_draw"]
    cells = [f"{pdr[str(i)]['ratio']:.3f}" if str(i) in pdr else "—" for i in (1, 2, 3, 0)]
    print(f"| {n} | " + " | ".join(cells) + f" | {r['mean_over_draws']:.3f} | [{r['ci90'][0]:.3f}, {r['ci90'][1]:.3f}] | {r['verdict']} |")
print()
print(": Ratios of seed-mean errors per draw at 210 training cases; the interval is the two-sided 90% t-interval over the three campaign draws. {#tbl-campaigns-draw-ratios-210}")
```

At 210 cases both orderings stand with intervals about half as wide, and
the baselines trade places: GeoTransolver, the weaker baseline at 35
cases, is the stronger at 210 (0.87 of ISLA's error against Transolver's
0.90), so its advantage over ISLA on HiLift grows with data while
Transolver's shrinks. The weights-off ablation's gain is 8% on every draw
(0.90–0.93), stable where it was draw-dependent at 35 cases, and remains
the measured in-distribution cost of the measure semantics rather than a
configuration. The draw still outweighs the seed for the two baselines
and ISLA (2.7–7.6x) but no longer for the ablation (1.8x), so the
two-seed protocol's understatement of uncertainty shrinks with the rung
without disappearing.

## Equivariance under random poses (campaign B) {#sec-campaigns-pose}

Every benchmark in the ISLA program presents geometries in one canonical
frame, so the architecture's exact SE(3) covariance had never had a chance
to earn accuracy. POSE-BENCH rotates every DrivAerML training and
validation case by an independent, fixed, uniformly random SO(3) rotation
(a deterministic function of the case, so the posed validation set is the
same benchmark for every architecture), trains GeoTransolver and Transolver
with uniform SO(3) rotation augmentation at unit drive, and ISLA as is
(@sec-nb-campb-verdict; preregistration in `studies/campaign_b_pose/`).
The canonical-frame references are float32 evaluations of the same
architectures' canonical runs.

```{python}
#| output: asis
import json
from pathlib import Path
d = json.loads(Path("studies/campaign_b_pose/campaign_b_fp32_2026-09-10.json").read_text())
A, C = d["arms"], d["canonical"]
rows = [("GeoTransolver + SO(3) augmentation", "gt_aug", "gt"), ("Transolver + SO(3) augmentation (lr 3e-3)", "transolver_aug", "transolver_lr3e3"),
        ("ISLA, no augmentation", "isla", "isla"), ("GeoTransolver, no augmentation (control)", "gt_noaug", "gt"), ("ISLA + SO(3) augmentation (contract check)", "isla_aug", "isla")]
print("| arm | seeds | posed pressure | canonical pressure | posed ÷ canonical | posed wall shear |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for n, a, c in rows:
    p, cc = A[a]["pressure_mean"], C[c]["pressure_mean"]
    print(f"| {n} | {A[a]['n_seeds_done']} | {p:.4f} | {cc:.4f} | {p / cc:.2f} | {A[a]['wss_mean']:.4f} |")
print()
print(": Surface-pressure relative L2 on the 48 DrivAerML validation cars, float32 inference, seed means; posed = every case in its own random SO(3) pose for training and validation; canonical = the same architecture trained and scored in the dataset's frame (unit-drive GeoTransolver over three seeds, Transolver over two, ISLA over three). Data: studies/campaign_b_pose/campaign_b_fp32_2026-09-10.json. {#tbl-campaigns-pose}")
```

Equivariance earns accuracy on every preregistered clause: the augmented
baselines lose more than 10% when poses vary (GeoTransolver +20%,
Transolver +31%), ISLA stays within 3% of its canonical error (+1.4%), and
posed ISLA leads the posed augmented GeoTransolver by 6% and Transolver by
19%, past the 5% bar. The no-augmentation GeoTransolver control shows what
augmentation buys at this data size: 4 points of a 25% loss. The result
reverses the canonical ordering, where ISLA is 10% behind GeoTransolver in
float32, so the value of exact equivariance is conditional on the
deployment: pose-normalized data do not need it, data in arbitrary frames
do. One clause is recorded as miscalibrated rather than met: the augmented
ISLA (0.0578) was required to fall inside the two unaugmented ISLA seeds
(0.0562–0.0571) and lands 1.2% above them; it is within the 3% used
everywhere else in the preregistration and within the canonical ISLA's own
3.8% seed spread, and the pose transform's covariance is unit-tested to
roundoff, so the posed numbers stand with that caveat.

## Interior carriers at matched parameters (campaign D) {#sec-campaigns-interior}

In float32 the reference ISLA query-token configuration (hidden 256, about
15M parameters) trails the unit-drive GeoTransolver-volume (27.6M) on
interior pressure by 6% and on eddy viscosity by 27% while leading on
velocity by 27%. Campaign D asked what carries each gap: ISLA at hidden
344, matching GeoTransolver-volume's parameter count, and
GeoTransolver-volume without its six-radius local features
(@sec-nb-campd-verdict; bars in @sec-nb-campaign).

```{python}
#| output: asis
import json
from pathlib import Path
d = json.loads(Path("studies/computational_support/campaign_d_verdict_2026-09-10.json").read_text())["per_arm"]
rows = [("ISLA query tokens + SDF, hidden 256 (reference, 15M)", "isla_qtsdfval"), ("ISLA query tokens + SDF, hidden 344 (27.6M)", "isla_qtsdf_h344"),
        ("GeoTransolver-volume, unit drive (reference, 27.6M)", "udrv_gt_vol"), ("GeoTransolver-volume, unit drive, no local features", "gt_vol_nolocal")]
print("| arm | seeds | pressure | velocity | eddy viscosity |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|")
for n, k in rows:
    m = d[k]["mean"]
    print(f"| {n} | {len(d[k]['seeds'])} | {m['pressure_l2']:.4f} | {m['velocity_l2']:.4f} | {m['nut_l2']:.4f} |")
print()
print(": Interior relative L2 on the 48 DrivAerML validation cars, float32 inference, same sampled points, two-seed means. Data: studies/computational_support/campaign_d_verdict_2026-09-10.json. {#tbl-campaigns-interior}")
```

Width does most of the work on ISLA's side: at matched parameters ISLA
leads GeoTransolver-volume on pressure (0.0497 against 0.0513) and on
velocity (0.0729 against 0.1070), and its eddy-viscosity gap narrows from
27% to 18%, between the preregistered "parameters carry the deficit" bar
(within 10%) and its falsifier (25% or worse). So the program book's
interior-pressure ordering is a parameter-budget statement: ISLA is behind
at 15M and ahead at 27.6M, for about 1.3x the step time. On
GeoTransolver's side the local features are a general 4–7% carrier and not
the source of its eddy-viscosity lead (removing them costs 5% on that
field against a 10% bar), nor of its bf16 inflation, which is unchanged
without them. The remaining eddy-viscosity gap is unexplained by either
arm, and it is not an input difference: both models receive the same
per-point geometry at the interior queries (position, signed distance and
its gradient direction; GeoTransolver as raw channels through a per-point
network, ISLA through invariant products with its anchors and the drive).
A wall-distance band decomposition of the saved predictions locates the
gap (@sec-nb-bands): in the near-wall band that holds 77% of the points,
ISLA at matched parameters and GeoTransolver-volume are equal on eddy
viscosity (0.081 against 0.080) and ISLA leads in the intermediate band;
the entire deficit is in the far field (SDF ≥ 0.05 L, 10% of the points),
where ISLA's eddy-viscosity error is 0.093 against 0.068 and which carries
46% of ISLA's squared error against 36% of GeoTransolver's. The same
far-field pattern holds for pressure and velocity but is invisible in
their totals, which are 90–94% near-wall. So at matched parameters ISLA
wins wherever the surface is close and GeoTransolver wins where it is far,
which pointed at geometry rather than a closure input: far from the body
every surface anchor looks alike, so ISLA's anchor-relative invariants
might lose resolution where a per-point network on raw position keeps it.

That reading was tested and falsified (@sec-nb-wake-verdict; preregistration
`studies/computational_support/PREREG_WAKE.md`). Two kinds of far-field
context tokens were added to the hidden-344 configuration, each in two
seeds: wake tokens, three interacting anchors on the drive axis at one,
two and four body half-extents downstream (over the rear deck, in the near
wake, and 0.7 body lengths behind the car), and latent volume tokens,
off-surface anchors along each slice anchor's normal, as the control for
"any off-surface context". Both constructions are covariant and invariant
to how the surface was sampled.

```{python}
#| output: asis
import json
from pathlib import Path
d = json.loads(Path("studies/computational_support/band_decomposition_wake_2026-09-10.json").read_text())["arms"]
rows = [("ISLA hidden 344 (reference)", "isla_h344"), ("ISLA hidden 344 + wake tokens", "isla_h344_wake"),
        ("ISLA hidden 344 + latent volume tokens", "isla_h344_lvt"), ("GeoTransolver-volume, unit drive", "gt_unit")]
ref = d["isla_h344"]["mean"]["nut"]["sdf>=0.05L"]["rel_l2"]; gt = d["gt_unit"]["mean"]["nut"]["sdf>=0.05L"]["rel_l2"]
print("| arm | eddy viscosity, near wall (SDF < 0.01 L) | eddy viscosity, 0.01–0.05 L | eddy viscosity, far field (≥ 0.05 L) | far-field gap closed | pressure, far field | velocity, far field |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for n, k in rows:
    m = d[k]["mean"]; far = m["nut"]["sdf>=0.05L"]["rel_l2"]
    seeds = ", ".join(f"{r['nut']['sdf>=0.05L']['rel_l2']:.3f}" for r in d[k]["runs"].values())
    closed = "—" if k in ("isla_h344", "gt_unit") else f"{(ref - far) / (ref - gt):+.0%}"
    print(f"| {n} | {m['nut']['sdf<0.01L']['rel_l2']:.3f} | {m['nut']['0.01-0.05L']['rel_l2']:.3f} | {far:.3f} ({seeds}) | {closed} | {m['pressure']['sdf>=0.05L']['rel_l2']:.3f} | {m['velocity']['sdf>=0.05L']['rel_l2']:.3f} |")
print()
print(": Relative L2 by signed-distance band, per-case values averaged over the 48 DrivAerML validation cars, float32, two-seed means (far-field seeds in parentheses). Preregistered bars on the far-field eddy viscosity: ≤ 0.074 supported, ≥ 0.085 falsified. Data: studies/computational_support/band_decomposition_wake_2026-09-10.json. {#tbl-campaigns-wake}")
```

Wake tokens close a fifth of the far-field gap and stop above the
falsifier; latent volume tokens widen it. Neither touches the near-wall or
intermediate bands, the far-field pressure and velocity, or the training
cost (wake tokens: none; latent volume tokens: 6% in step time and
memory). So the far-field eddy-viscosity deficit is not an
anchor-resolution effect, and two diagnostics on the artifacts close that
class of explanation (@sec-nb-far-wake). A distance-shell decomposition
shows ISLA *ahead* of GeoTransolver-volume on eddy viscosity in every far
shell out to 0.4 L and behind only beyond it, downstream (0.108 against
0.071 on 2.2% of the points), most of all beside the car. A routing-mass
probe of the trained checkpoints shows the slice anchors were never
surface anchors: interior query tokens dominate over 220 of the 256 slices
in every layer of the reference model, and in the wake-token model the
three tokens took up to 71 slice-units and pushed up to 89 anchors
downstream of the rear, with a 6% effect on the far wake. So the deficit
is a far-wake structure that ISLA predicts worse than GeoTransolver-volume
regardless of where its anchors are, and no repair is in hand. Two
hypotheses are recorded without a launch: under-sampling of the far wake
in the training queries (a measure-consistent oversampling would test it)
and, weaker, that ISLA's query seed holds the downstream coordinate only
implicitly, as a product of two of its channels.

## Convention conditioning on the fastback shift (campaign C, T1) {#sec-campaigns-conditioning}

If two vehicle families with different simulation conventions (solver,
ground and wheel treatment) are trained together, does telling the model
which convention a case follows help it keep them apart? T1 trains ISLA and
the unit-drive GeoTransolver on all 435 DrivAerML cars plus the 794 SHIFT-SUV
estate cars, with and without a constant per-cell convention flag (0 for
DrivAerML, 1 for SHIFT-SUV; a boundary scalar for ISLA, a seventh functional
channel for GeoTransolver), and scores both zero-shot on the 99 fastback
validation cases, which carry the flag value 1 (@sec-nb-campc-t1-verdict).

```{python}
#| output: asis
import json
from pathlib import Path
d = json.loads(Path("studies/campaign_c_transfer/campaign_c_t1_2026-09-10.json").read_text())["arms"]
rows = [("ISLA, no flag", "cond0_isla"), ("ISLA, convention flag", "cond1_isla"),
        ("GeoTransolver (unit drive), no flag", "cond0_gt"), ("GeoTransolver (unit drive), convention flag", "cond1_gt")]
print("| arm | seeds | fastback pressure | fastback wall shear | fastback drag rel. MAE | DrivAerML pressure |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for n, k in rows:
    a = d[k]; f = a["fastback"]; dr = a.get("drivaer") or {}
    print(f"| {n} | {a['n_seeds']} | {f['pressure_l2']:.3f} | {f['wss_l2']:.3f} | {f['CD_rel_mae']:.3f} | {dr.get('pressure_l2', float('nan')):.4f} |")
print()
print(": Float32 inference, seed means over two seeds; every arm trains on 435 DrivAerML + 794 estate cars for 500 epochs at lr 1e-3. Drag is the recipe's integrated drag coefficient, mean absolute error over the reference mean (0.75). Data: studies/campaign_c_transfer/campaign_c_t1_2026-09-10.json. {#tbl-campaigns-conditioning}")
```

The flag is worth nothing: the fastback error moves by 1% (ISLA) and 5%
(GeoTransolver) in the wrong direction, inside or at the seed spread, and
the in-family DrivAerML error by 1–2%. The preregistered NULL clause holds
for ISLA and GeoTransolver lands at its edge, on the side of no help. The
conventions differ in the flow the surface sees, which both models read
from the geometry and the field they fit, so a one-bit label carries no
information the inputs lack; what the estate family buys the fastback
cases is coverage, not identification.

The unconditioned arms also answer a question the diversity result below
leaves open: how much of the in-family cost of mixing is the mixing itself
when the source data is not halved. With all 435 DrivAerML cars kept,
adding 794 estate cars raises the DrivAerML error 17% for ISLA and 4% for
GeoTransolver. Against the half-and-half mix (8% and 4%), ISLA's mixing
cost grows with the foreign share and GeoTransolver's does not, and the
extra 577 estate cars improve the fastback error by only 6–9% over the
217-car mix, so the sibling family's coverage saturates within a few
hundred cases.

## Matched-count diversity on the fastback shift (campaign C, T2) {#sec-campaigns-diversity}

With the training set held at 435 cases, replacing half of the DrivAerML
cars with SHIFT-SUV estate cars asks what family coverage is worth at a
fixed label budget. Both arms are scored zero-shot on the 99 SHIFT-SUV
fastback validation cases, a third family seen by neither, and on the
DrivAerML validation cars (@sec-nb-campc-t2-verdict).

```{python}
#| output: asis
import json
from pathlib import Path
d = json.loads(Path("studies/campaign_c_transfer/campaign_c_t2_2026-09-10.json").read_text())["arms"]
rows = [("ISLA, 435 DrivAerML (single-family reference)", "ref_single_isla"), ("ISLA, 218 DrivAerML + 217 estate", "mix435_isla"),
        ("GeoTransolver (unit drive), 435 DrivAerML (single-family reference)", "ref_single_gt"), ("GeoTransolver (unit drive), 218 DrivAerML + 217 estate", "mix435_gt")]
print("| arm | seeds | fastback pressure | fastback wall shear | fastback drag rel. MAE | DrivAerML pressure |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for n, k in rows:
    a = d[k]; f = a["fastback"]; dr = a.get("drivaer") or {}
    print(f"| {n} | {a['n_seeds']} | {f['pressure_l2']:.3f} | {f['wss_l2']:.3f} | {f['CD_rel_mae']:.2f} | {dr.get('pressure_l2', float('nan')):.4f} |")
print()
print(": Float32 inference, seed means over two seeds; the single-family references are the program's existing DrivAerML checkpoints evaluated under the code snapshot that wrote them. Drag is the recipe's integrated drag coefficient, mean absolute error over the reference mean (0.75). Data: studies/campaign_c_transfer/campaign_c_t2_2026-09-10.json. {#tbl-campaigns-diversity}")
```

Diversity helps on the target far past the bar and costs the source far
past its bar, for both architectures: the fastback error falls 84% (ISLA)
and 81% (GeoTransolver), the drag error from unusable to 13–16%, while the
DrivAerML error rises 32% and 19% against a 10% bar. The preregistered
"helps" clause is therefore not met and the result is a trade: at a fixed
label budget, half the labels spent on the target convention's sibling
family buy the target family almost entirely (the mixed 435-case models
match the program's earlier DrivAerML + 794-estate training on the
fastback cases) and cost a fifth to a third of the source family's
accuracy. Four control lanes trained on the same 218 DrivAerML cars alone
split that cost: the halving of the source data accounts for a factor 1.23
(ISLA) and 1.14 (GeoTransolver), the mixing itself for 1.08 and 1.04
(products 1.32 and 1.19, the measured costs). So the foreign family costs
the source family only 4–8% at this share; the rest is the data ladder.
ISLA pays more on both factors, the same direction as the few-shot result
below.

## Few-shot adaptation on the fastback shift (campaign C, T3) {#sec-campaigns-fewshot}

The DrivAerML → SHIFT-SUV fastback shift is the program's one real
transfer setting: both architectures fail zero-shot (@sec-controls), and
the only known repair was training on the full 794-case estate family
(0.11–0.13 on the 99 fastback validation cases). T3 asks the practical
question: given 20 labelled fastback cases, does a source-only DrivAerML
checkpoint adapt better than a model trained from scratch on the same 20
cases for the same 1,000 optimizer steps? The preregistered fine-tuning
rate was 1e-4 against 1e-3 for scratch; a sensitivity arm at the matched
rate 1e-3 was added, with its bars, after the first readout showed the
1e-4 fine-tune under-adapted (@sec-nb-campc-t3, @sec-nb-campc-t3-verdict).

```{python}
#| output: asis
import json
from pathlib import Path
d = json.loads(Path("studies/campaign_c_transfer/campaign_c_t3_2026-09-10.json").read_text())["arms"]
rows = [("ISLA, fine-tuned from the DrivAerML reference, lr 1e-4 (preregistered)", "ft20_isla"),
        ("ISLA, fine-tuned, lr 1e-3 (matched to scratch)", "ft20lr3_isla"),
        ("ISLA, from scratch on the 20 cases, lr 1e-3", "scratch20_isla"),
        ("GeoTransolver (unit drive), fine-tuned, lr 1e-4 (preregistered)", "ft20_gt"),
        ("GeoTransolver, fine-tuned, lr 1e-3 (matched to scratch)", "ft20lr3_gt"),
        ("GeoTransolver, from scratch on the 20 cases, lr 1e-3", "scratch20_gt")]
print("| arm | seeds | fastback pressure | fastback wall shear | drag-coefficient relative MAE |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|")
for n, k in rows:
    a = d[k]; f = a["fastback"]
    print(f"| {n} | {a['n_seeds']} | {f['pressure_l2']:.3f} | {f['wss_l2']:.3f} | {f['CD_rel_mae']:.3f} |")
print()
print(": Relative L2 on the 99 SHIFT-SUV fastback validation cases (never used for adaptation), float32 inference, seed means over two fine-tuning seeds; every arm trains 1,000 optimizer steps at batch four on the same 20 cases. The drag coefficient is the recipe's integrated surface traction, mean absolute error over the reference mean (0.75). Data: studies/campaign_c_transfer/campaign_c_t3_2026-09-10.json. {#tbl-campaigns-fewshot}")
```

At the matched learning rate the two architectures separate cleanly.
GeoTransolver's DrivAerML pretraining is worth 31% (0.128 fine-tuned
against 0.186 from scratch), and the adapted model reaches the level the
program had only reached by retraining on 1,229 mixed cases, from 20 + 10
labels in about five minutes on one node. ISLA's pretraining is worth
nothing: 0.187 fine-tuned against 0.198 from scratch, inside the 5%
"worth nothing" clause of the sensitivity arm's bars up to rounding. The
scratch arms agree (0.19–0.20), so the architectures learn the same amount
from the target data and differ only in what they carry over from
DrivAerML. The preregistered "credible fallback" bar (≤ 0.15 and ≥ 2x
over scratch) is met by no arm, GeoTransolver passing the level and
missing the ratio; the preregistered 1e-4 fine-tunes were under-adapted
(ISLA 2.3x worse than scratch), which is why the sensitivity arm exists.

This is the third independent measurement in this program pointing the
same way: ISLA's zero-shot fastback force error of 1.6x
(@sec-controls-offset), the constant-gauge ISLA's collapse under density
skew (@sec-campaigns-density), and now a transfer value of zero for its
DrivAerML pretraining. What ISLA learns on DrivAerML is specific to
DrivAerML's conventions in a way GeoTransolver's representation is not,
and that is the concrete target for the architectural directions of this
program. The first training batch makes the same point from the other
end: the pretrained ISLA starts at a loss of 0.194 against 0.477 for a
random initialization (2.5x better) and the pretrained GeoTransolver at
0.176 against 0.278 (1.6x), so both carry DrivAerML knowledge worth about
the same at step 0; after 1,000 matched-rate steps ISLA's head start has
shrunk to 6% and GeoTransolver's has grown to 31%. Caveats: one source
checkpoint per architecture (the ISLA source is the lr 3e-3 reference, the
GeoTransolver source the unit-drive lr 1e-3 run) and a two-point
learning-rate grid; a different rate or a warm-up could move either number
but not the sign of the difference at matched rate. The initialization
itself was verified: a frozen copy of the ISLA source loaded through the
fine-tuning hook reproduces the source's zero-shot fastback error to four
digits (@sec-nb-snapshot-resolved).

## Density robustness against fair baselines (campaign E) {#sec-campaigns-density}

The program book's remaining robustness claim for ISLA was that its
similarity gauge makes the prediction insensitive to how densely the
surface is sampled: on the 48 DrivAerML validation cars, a Poisson-biased
draw with ten times the inclusion probability on the front half of the car
(exact Horvitz–Thompson weights carried in the measure field, total measure
preserved) raised the gauge arm's pressure error only from 0.063 to 0.076,
a factor 1.20. The audit's objection was that no input-matched baseline had
been run through the same probe. Campaign E ran it, in float32 inference
(@sec-nb-campe-verdict for the preregistration and the bf16 preview), on
the canonical unit-drive GeoTransolver and Transolver checkpoints and on
three ISLA configurations.

The probe has one convention that matters for models reading absolute
coordinates. The original probe centred the mesh before the biased draw, so
GeoTransolver and Transolver saw the unbiased pool's frame (the "pool
frame"); a biased mesher would instead deliver the mean of the points it
produced (the "sample frame", the program's canonical convention since
2026-09-10, @sec-nb-campe-frame). ISLA centres internally on the drawn
sample and is invariant to the choice. Both conventions are reported; the
sample frame is the one to quote.

```{python}
#| output: asis
import json
from pathlib import Path
d = json.loads(Path("studies/campaign_e_evalonly/campaign_e_density_fp32_2026-09-09.json").read_text())
s = json.loads(Path("studies/campaign_e_evalonly/campaign_e_density_fp32_sampleframe_2026-09-10.json").read_text())
b = json.loads(Path("studies/campaign_e_evalonly/campaign_e_density_bf16_2026-09-09.json").read_text())
names = {"gt_unit": "GeoTransolver, unit drive", "transolver_unit": "Transolver, unit drive (lr 3e-3)",
         "isla_reference": "ISLA, constant gauge (reference configuration)", "isla_gauge": "ISLA, similarity gauge",
         "isla_noweights": "ISLA, measure weights off (ablation)"}
print("| arm | seeds | uniform draw | 10:1 biased draw, sample frame | factor, sample frame (per seed) | factor, pool frame (per seed) | bf16 uniform draw |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for k, n in names.items():
    a = d["arms"][k]; sa = s["arms"][k]; ab = b["arms"][k]
    seeds = ", ".join(f"{x:.2f}" for x in a["factor_seeds"]); sseeds = ", ".join(f"{x:.2f}" for x in sa["factor_seeds"])
    print(f"| {n} | {sa['n_seeds']} | {sa['unif_pressure_mean']:.4f} | {sa['biased_pressure_mean']:.3f} | {sa['factor_mean']:.2f} ({sseeds}) | {a['factor_mean']:.2f} ({seeds}) | {ab['unif_pressure_mean']:.4f} |")
print()
print(": Surface-pressure relative L2 on the 48 DrivAerML validation cars, float32 inference, seed means; the factor is the biased-draw error divided by the uniform-draw error. Sample frame: the mesh is centred after the biased draw (the program's canonical probes drivaer_probe_{unif2,biased3}_sf); pool frame: centred before it (the original probes). The uniform-draw levels agree between frames to 0.0002 and the sample-frame ones are shown. The last column is the pool-frame uniform-draw evaluation in bf16, kept for the program's per-architecture offset table. Data: studies/campaign_e_evalonly/campaign_e_density_fp32_sampleframe_2026-09-10.json (sample frame; four baseline runs read from the generalization session's evaluations of the same yaml), campaign_e_density_fp32_2026-09-09.json (pool frame) and campaign_e_density_bf16_2026-09-09.json. {#tbl-campaigns-density}")
```

The claim holds against fair baselines, by a wide margin: the
preregistered bar asked for a GeoTransolver factor of at least 1.32 with
the gauge arm's factor at most 1.24, and the sample-frame readout is 12.1
against 1.21 (pool frame 9.5 against 1.21). Every car is worse under the
bias for every run of the four non-gauge arms. In the sample frame the two
baselines and the constant-gauge ISLA collapse alike, to roughly twelve
times their uniform-draw error; the pool frame had flattered Transolver
(3.9) and GeoTransolver (9.5) by handing them the unbiased pool's centre,
a quantity a biased mesher cannot supply. The three ISLA configurations
move by at most 1% between frames, the internal centering being exactly
what makes them frame-independent. The cost of the robustness is visible
in the first column: the gauge arm is 10–20% less accurate on the uniform
draw than the constant-gauge ISLA (0.0560) and the unit-drive
GeoTransolver (0.0504), so the trade is a fifth of the accuracy on a
well-sampled surface for a ten-fold smaller error under the skew. The
measure-weights-off ablation is the least robust of the five, and, reading
the mesher's sampling density in place of the surface measure and is 2.8%
more accurate on canonical data for it, reaches an error above 1.0 under
the bias, worse than predicting zero. That is the discretization dependence
of a density-reading model made visible: the ablation measures what the
measure semantics cost in-distribution and what they buy under a
discretization change, and it is a diagnostic, not a candidate
configuration (program ruling of 2026-09-10, @sec-nb-redirect).

The mechanism, stated as the reading the numbers support rather than as a
separately tested result: the gauge normalizes ISLA's kernel by the local
measure, so the Horvitz–Thompson weights act as a quadrature correction and
the field is reconstructed from the sparse half nearly as well as from the
dense half; the constant-gauge ISLA meets weights far outside its training
range in every measure-weighted sum; the weights-off ISLA has no measure
and reads the front-heavy token cloud as geometry; GeoTransolver's
radius-based local features are neighbour statistics that shift ten-fold
with density, and both it and Transolver read absolute coordinates whose
origin moves with the sample's centre of mass under the bias. The
pool-frame reading that Transolver's routing "degrades more gracefully"
(3.9 against 9.5) was an artefact of that frame: given the centre a biased
mesher would deliver, Transolver degrades as much as GeoTransolver. A gauge
arm with weights off would test whether the gauge alone suffices; it is
not scheduled.

One preregistration miscalibration is recorded rather than rewritten: the
"holds" clause named the ISLA reference configuration as the arm whose
factor had to stay within 1.24, but the book's 1.20 belongs to the gauge
arm, so the clause as written could not be met; the gauge arm is graded in
its place. A second, program-wide observation from the same evaluations:
bf16 inference inflates the uniform-draw error by 8.5–9.7% for
GeoTransolver and Transolver but only 2.8–4.0% for the three ISLA
configurations, so every bf16 comparison in the program has penalized the
baselines about 5% more than ISLA, which is one reason the program moved
to float32 as its reporting instrument.
